reader.summary: The dominant story this week was the resolution of the Credit Suisse bonus dispute: Swiss top court definitively ruled against former CS bankers who sought to recover bonuses stripped after the UBS takeover, closing a long legal battle. In the same week Credit Suisse secured 800 million dollars from insurers in the Greensill settlement. These rulings appeared to sharpen a broader regulatory strain: multiple reports indicated UBS was actively exploring the option of relocating its headquarters outside Switzerland if capital and regulatory rules tightened further, a move a domestic competitor warned would be damaging for the country. In Zurich, FIFA president Gianni Infantino faced rebelling members following a failed attempt to sell a World Cup-related stake. On the economic front, Switzerland's finance minister warned that steep European debt levels risked triggering a new euro-area crisis, and the federal government approved emergency reserve fuel withdrawals at Zurich Airport amid a supply shortage. A Swiss journalist faced the prospect of a criminal court sentence for having exposed a top banker. In lighter news, Novak Djokovic accepted a wild-card invitation to the Swiss Indoors, a Swiss solar-powered aircraft's altitude record was officially confirmed, Swisscom prevailed in an antitrust appeal over its fiber-network expansion, and the country's trade chief clarified that a recent Rolex-and-gold gift was for the United States rather than a personal gesture toward the president.

display.eli5:
Here is what is happening in Switzerland right now. The big story is that UBS, the giant bank, is seriously thinking about moving its headquarters out of the country. It is angry about capital rules the government set after it took over Credit Suisse, and it is telling the world it might leave. Think of it as your school threatening to move to a different town because it does not like the rules.

At the same time, a journalist who did the right thing by exposing a shady banker is about to get her court verdict. If she gets sentenced, it could be seen as punishing people for telling the truth about powerful people.

What will probably happen next: the government will have to make a move on the UBS situation, either softening the rules to keep the bank or toughening its stance and risking its departure. And the fuel problem at Zurich Airport will keep causing flight chaos for travelers.

What would be a surprise: the parliament suddenly announcing who will replace the finance minister who just resigned, which would add a whole new political layer to an already stressful week.
